definition: An anxiety hierarchy is an ordered set of feared situations or cues, arranged to match a person’s level of anxiety from less distressing to more distressing. In exposure-based therapy, it is used to tailor and control practice so feared situations can be introduced, repeated, or prolonged in a graded way.

reasons: The packet supports that exposure scenarios can be tailored to a patient’s anxiety hierarchy, but it does not define an anxiety hierarchy as an ordered set of feared situations or as arranged from less distressing to more distressing.

The claim that it is used in exposure-based therapy to introduce, repeat, or prolong feared situations in a graded way goes beyond the packet; the source only says situations can be selectively designed and purposefully repeated or prolonged to fit the patient’s hierarchy.
The definition adds general therapy guidance that is not explicitly supported by the supplied text.

The packet supports that exposure scenarios were “individually tailored to the patients’ anxiety hierarchy” and that VRET has high situational/therapeutic control so scenarios can be “selectively designed and purposefully repeated or prolonged” to fit patients’ anxiety hierarchy, but it does not define an anxiety hierarchy as an “ordered set” or specify ordering “from less distressing to more distressing.”

The definition’s phrasing that the hierarchy is an “ordered set of feared situations or cues” is not explicitly stated in the packet text provided; the packet only mentions exposure scenarios tailored to an anxiety hierarchy.
